questions.question: When does a destructuring default value apply? Why does `const { age = 30 } = { age: null }` produce `null`?
questions.answer: A default applies only when the incoming value is `undefined` — either the key is missing or its value is explicitly `undefined`. `null` is a real value, so the default is skipped and `age` becomes `null`. The same rule applies to array destructuring and function parameter defaults. Use `age ?? 30` if you also want to replace `null`.
key_points: Defaults trigger on `undefined` only.
Missing keys count as `undefined`.
`null` skips the default.
Use `??` when `null` should also fall back.

questions.question: Explain the difference between rest and spread, even though both use `...`.
questions.answer: Rest appears on the left side of an assignment or in a parameter list and **collects** the remaining values into a new array or object. Spread appears on the right side, in an array/object literal, or at a call site and **expands** an iterable or object's own enumerable properties into individual values. Rest must be last; spread can appear anywhere in a literal and can be repeated.
key_points: Left side / parameters → rest collects.
Right side / literals / calls → spread expands.
Rest must be the final element.
Both create new containers but only shallowly.

questions.question: Are spread copies deep or shallow? What happens to nested objects, and what should you use for a real deep clone?
questions.answer: Spread is a shallow copy: it creates a new outer array or object, but nested objects and arrays are copied by reference. Mutating a nested value through the copy is visible through the original. For data-only deep clones use `structuredClone(value)`; it handles nested objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, and `Date`, but not functions, DOM nodes, or class prototypes.
key_points: New container, shared nested references.
Top-level changes are isolated; nested changes are not.
`structuredClone` is the modern deep clone for data.
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` loses `undefined`, functions, and types.

key_points: Destructure in the parameter list with per-field defaults.
The trailing `= {}` makes the whole argument optional.
Without `= {}`, calling with no argument throws.

questions.answer: It throws `TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'name' of 'undefined'`. The pattern requires `user` to be an object before it can read `name`; the source has no `user`, so the nested read targets `undefined`. Fix by defaulting the intermediate object: `const { user: { name = 'Kakade' } = {} } = {};` — the `= {}` supplies an empty object when `user` is missing.
key_points: Each nesting level is dereferenced.
A missing intermediate object throws `TypeError`.
Default the intermediate with `= {}`.
A default on the leaf (`name = ...`) does not guard the parent.

questions.answer: It logs `Mumbai`. Object spread creates a new outer object but copies `address` by reference, so both objects point to the same nested object. Use `structuredClone(original)` for a deep copy, or spread the nested object explicitly (`{ ...original, address: { ...original.address } }`) when you only need one level deeper.
key_points: Spread is shallow.
Nested objects are shared by reference.
`structuredClone` performs a deep clone for data.
Explicit nested spread works for known, shallow structures.
